  "text": "The council sent a man to disconnect my father’s shadow.

“He’s been dead eight months,” I said.

The man checked his tablet.

“And you’ve continued using it.”

Behind me, Dad’s shadow sat at the kitchen table. Mine stood where it should, attached to my feet.

“I didn’t know who to call.”

“Most people don’t.”

He unpacked a yellow scraper and a roll of black bags.

Since the funeral, the shadow had kept Dad’s hours. Downstairs at six. By the back door after lunch. In his armchair until the shipping forecast ended.

Sometimes I put the radio on for it.

“Does it hurt?” I asked.

“Not the shadow.”

He moved the table aside. Dad’s outline stayed seated, its hands folded over an invisible stomach.

The man knelt and worked the scraper under one shoe.

Upstairs, a floorboard creaked.

He stopped.

“Anyone else home?”

“No.”

Another creak. Directly above us.

The man lowered the scraper carefully.

“Did you let it upstairs?”

“It’s his house.”

He looked towards the ceiling.

“How many nights?”

“Every night.”

The shadow unfolded its hands.

The man packed his tools, leaving the black bags on the floor.

“Wait,” I said. “You haven’t finished.”

“I can’t disconnect an occupied service.”

From upstairs came a cough I recognised. Then the squeal of Dad’s bed springs.

The man hurried out, pulling the front door shut behind him.

I stood in the kitchen until footsteps reached the landing.

“Who was that?” Dad called.

His shadow rose and stretched towards the stairs.

“Council,” I said.

“Don’t let them in again.”

I heard him trying each bedroom door.

“Which one’s yours now?”"
